topic.title: ADHD
topic.subtitle: Neurobiology, behavioral impact, and evidence-based parenting approaches

heroStat.label: Heritability across twin studies
heroStat.detail: ADHD is one of the most heritable behavioral conditions in medicine — it runs in families more than almost any other condition.

quickStats.label: Delay in cortical maturation
quickStats.detail: Longitudinal NIH research found children with ADHD show a delay in prefrontal cortex maturation of roughly 3–5 years. A 15-year-old may be operating with the self-regulation capacity of a 10 or 11-year-old.

quickStats.label: Continue to meet criteria in adolescence
Carry significant functional impairment into adulthood
Effect size for stimulant medication
quickStats.detail: Among the largest effect sizes of any psychiatric pharmacotherapy.

quickStats.label: Male-to-female diagnosis ratio (clinical samples)
quickStats.detail: Community samples show a smaller gap (1.6:1), suggesting underidentification in girls.

whereExpertsDisagree.title: Where Experts Disagree (or the evidence is still developing)
whereExpertsDisagree.description: Claims below are split into what current research supports strongly versus what should be held more loosely.

rows.strongClaim: ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder with strong genetic heritability (~74–76%); neuroimaging shows consistent, replicated structural and functional differences vs. neurotypical brains.
rows.softerClaim: Brain imaging findings are group-level findings — they do not predict any individual child's outcome.

rows.strongClaim: Stimulant medication is the most effective single intervention, with robust effect sizes (0.8–1.0).
rows.softerClaim: Long-term outcomes of medication-only treatment remain uncertain — evidence beyond 3 years is limited and mixed.

rows.strongClaim: Some meta-analyses report effects on inattention and impulsivity.
rows.softerClaim: Methodological limitations (especially blinding) prevent a strong endorsement; classified Level 3, 'possibly efficacious.'

rows.strongClaim: Omega-3 supplementation shows modest, consistent effects in some studies, particularly for children with low baseline levels.
rows.softerClaim: Evidence is emerging/limited and likely benefits only a subgroup — not a primary intervention.

rows.strongClaim: Barkley's inhibition model (executive function deficits cascading from impaired inhibition) is consistently supported and widely used.
rows.softerClaim: The dual-pathway model (executive function + motivational pathways) is a dominant theoretical frame but remains a model, not a settled fact.

rows.strongClaim: Research Bible: 20–30% of children with ADHD have a co-occurring learning disability (Mayes & Calhoun, 2006) — the only rate in this chain backed by a specifically named, citable study.
rows.softerClaim: Parent Guide states ~46%, with no citation given. Presented as a softer, uncited claim rather than a competing peer-reviewed estimate. Flagged for reconciliation; both agree LD co-occurrence is common enough to warrant screening.

coOccurringConditions.title: Co-Occurring Conditions
coOccurringConditions.description: Co-occurring conditions in ADHD are the rule, not the exception.

rows.note: Most common pairing; largely maintained by coercive parenting cycles.
Can mimic inattention; stimulants may worsen anxiety in some children.
Parent guide cites ~46%, uncited — see 'Where Experts Disagree.' Needs psychoeducational testing to confirm.
Wide range depending on sample; increases behavioral complexity and complicates medication choice.
Requires specialist evaluation before stimulant initiation.

whatIsIt.title: What Is It?
whatIsIt.parent: ADHD is a highly heritable, chronic condition that affects the brain's ability to manage the demands of daily life — a disorder of self-management, not a behavior problem. It has nothing to do with intelligence; the issue is consistency and execution, not ability. More than half of kids diagnosed continue to struggle significantly as adults.
whatIsIt.practitioner: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder is a neurodevelopmental disorder (APA, 2022) characterized by persistent, developmentally inappropriate inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity causing functional impairment across settings. It is classified as a disorder of executive function and self-regulation, with heritability estimates of ~74–76% (Faraone et al., 2021) and robust, replicated neuroimaging differences in prefrontal cortex, basal ganglia, and dopaminergic/noradrenergic transmission (Cortese, 2012). It is not caused by poor parenting, screen time, sugar, or lack of discipline, though these can exacerbate symptoms in a predisposed child.

whatItMeansInYourKidsBrain.title: What It Means in Your Kid's Brain
whatItMeansInYourKidsBrain.parent: Two brain chemicals — dopamine and norepinephrine — act as fuel for focus, motivation, and self-regulation, and the ADHD brain doesn't maintain optimal levels of them consistently. That's why a teen can focus for hours on a video game (constant built-in feedback) but can't sustain attention on homework (no such feedback) — it's brain chemistry, not preference. Three key regions are involved: the prefrontal cortex (the brain's 'CEO' — planning, impulse control), the basal ganglia (the 'go signal' for starting tasks), and the cerebellum (coordinating scattered thinking). Researchers increasingly see ADHD as a network/connectivity issue — like poor cell signal — rather than one broken part.
whatItMeansInYourKidsBrain.practitioner: Core neurochemical substrate involves deficits in dopaminergic and noradrenergic signaling in prefrontal and subcortical circuits (Volkow et al., 2009): reduced DA receptor density in PFC and increased DA transporter activity in the striatum, causing rapid reuptake and insufficient signal duration. Barkley's (1997, 2015) inhibition model frames ADHD as a deficit in behavioral inhibition cascading into working memory, self-talk, emotion/motivation regulation, and flexible planning deficits. A distinct motivational pathway (mesolimbic dopamine system) explains why salience/immediacy of reward directly gates performance (Sonuga-Barke, 2003 dual-pathway model). Meta-analyses show volumetric reductions in PFC, caudate, putamen, and cerebellum, with cortical maturation delayed ~3–5 years in prefrontal regions (Shaw et al., 2007).

howToSupportThem.title: How to Support Them

parent.detail: Catch one specific thing your teen does well every day and name it. Build reward systems that are immediate — long-term rewards have almost no motivational value for the ADHD brain.

Break tasks into the smallest possible steps. Ask 'what's the very next thing you're going to do?' and get a specific answer. Think out loud together instead of solving it for them. Debrief without blame after something goes wrong.

Visual schedules and checklists, consistent time structures, 5-minute transition warnings, and reducing decision fatigue (set things out the night before) all reduce the demand on a brain that can't reliably self-structure.

A dysregulated parent's nervous system activates dysregulation in the teen (co-regulation). Pause before responding, separate the behavior from the relationship, and repair openly when you lose your patience.

howToSupportThem.practitioner: Behavioral Parent Training (BPT) is a well-established, Level 1 evidence-based intervention: clear one-step commands, immediate labeled praise, planned ignoring of minor attention-seeking behavior, consistent mild immediate consequences, and predictable routines. Effects are largest while intervention is active and are diminished when parents have untreated ADHD, depression, or trauma history (Chronis et al., 2004). Environmental scaffolding (visual schedules, external timers, reduced distractors, chunked tasks) reduces the demand on ADHD executive function and prevents the majority of ADHD-driven behavior problems.

whatToLearn.title: What to Learn: The Six Clusters
whatToLearn.description: Most teens with ADHD struggle in several of these areas at once.

clusters.athome: Sits down to do homework but scrolls their phone for an hour; knows it needs to be done but can't begin.
Gets distracted mid-sentence, loses track of conversations, needs every instruction repeated.
Falls asleep doing work, seems sluggish for no reason, can't maintain effort on boring tasks.
Explodes over small disappointments, can't let things go, gets overwhelmed when plans change.
Forgets what you said 5 minutes ago, loses things constantly, can't multi-step follow directions.
Acts without thinking, makes impulsive decisions, struggles to pause before responding.

whatToLearn.emotionalDysregulation: Deficient Emotional Self-Regulation (DESR) is now recognized as a core feature of ADHD, not a side effect. The emotional regulation 'hot circuit' is directly impaired, so emotions hit harder and faster with less buffer between feeling and reacting. This is not manipulation — it's an overflow, not a strategy.

practicalInfo.title: Practical Info: Treatment & School Supports

medication.stimulants: Methylphenidate (Ritalin, Concerta) and amphetamine salts (Adderall, Vyvanse) increase dopamine/norepinephrine availability in the prefrontal cortex. Most effective single intervention; effect sizes 0.8–1.0. Requires monitoring of heart rate, blood pressure, growth, sleep, and appetite; cardiology clearance needed with cardiac history.
medication.nonStimulants: Strattera (atomoxetine), Intuniv, and newer options like Viloxazine — a legitimate alternative for teens who don't respond well to stimulants. Take several weeks to build up in the system.
medication.whatMedicationCannotDo: Teach organization, planning, or time management; repair damaged relationships; eliminate all symptoms entirely; replace the need for supportive structure at home.

schoolSupports.plan504: Accommodations (extended time, preferential seating, reduced homework quantity, sensory breaks) — appropriate when ADHD impacts access to learning but specialized instruction isn't required.
schoolSupports.iep: Specialized instruction and related services (resource room, speech-language therapy, social skills groups) — required when ADHD significantly impairs academic performance. IEP quality accounts for ~25% of variance in child outcomes (Ruble et al., 2010) — push for specific, measurable, time-bound goals.

digitalTools: EndeavorRx — FDA-authorized video game-based attention therapy
Body doubling — having another person present while your teen works activates the brain's focus system
External reminders/systems — alarms, timers, checklists are prosthetics for working memory, not crutches

whatToPractice.title: What to Practice
dailyChecklist: Give one specific piece of praise today — name the behavior, not just the result
Provide a transition warning before any schedule change
Break any new task into the smallest possible first step
Check in after a hard moment: 'What do you need from me?'
End the day with one moment of connection — not about performance
minimalViablePracticePlan: One-step commands delivered with physical proximity and eye contact
A visual schedule or checklist for at least one high-conflict routine (morning or homework)
A specific, labeled praise contingency for one target behavior
One structural modification to the environment (reduce distractions, add timer, simplify task)
Contact with the child's teacher/school about current functioning and available supports
whatToPractice.note: These five elements, consistently applied, tend to produce observable change within 2–4 weeks.

specificSituationPaths.title: The Homework Battle
specificSituationPaths.scenario: An 8-year-old with ADHD-Combined starts homework, loses focus within 5 minutes, begins doodling, and melts down when redirected.
specificSituationPaths.whatsReallyHappening: A sustained attention and task re-engagement failure driven by executive function deficit, compounded by low motivation salience (homework is non-preferred) and insufficient external structure.
specificSituationPaths.response: Break homework into 10-minute chunks with 5-minute movement breaks. Use a visual timer. Do the hardest subject first when medication is most effective. Give immediate reinforcement for completed segments.

specificSituationPaths.title: The Morning Routine Meltdown
specificSituationPaths.scenario: Repeated verbal reminders about the morning routine stop working; the child loses track of the next step.
specificSituationPaths.whatsReallyHappening: Working memory deficit means the child loses track of the next step once distracted; the parent's voice becomes background noise through intermittent reinforcement.
specificSituationPaths.response: Create a visual, self-monitored morning checklist posted at eye level. Pair each step with a timer. Remove verbal reminders — let the environment prompt, not the parent.

specificSituationPaths.title: The After-School Crash
specificSituationPaths.scenario: A 7-year-old holds it together at school but explodes at home starting around 3:30 PM.
specificSituationPaths.whatsReallyHappening: 'After-school restraint collapse' — the child expends enormous regulatory energy masking symptoms at school; home is safe enough for the accumulated regulatory debt to surface. Medication may also be wearing off.
specificSituationPaths.response: Reduce demands for the first 30–60 minutes after school. Offer a snack, low-demand activity, and physical decompression time before homework or chores.

commonlyAskedQuestions.q: Is my teen just being lazy or defiant?
commonlyAskedQuestions.a: No. This is the core distinction: ADHD is a 'doing' problem, not a 'knowing' problem. Your teen genuinely intends to do the task; the part of the brain responsible for starting, sustaining, and completing that action is impaired ('point of performance' failure).

commonlyAskedQuestions.q: Why can my kid focus for hours on a video game but not on homework?
commonlyAskedQuestions.a: Video games are engineered for constant dopamine feedback — points, levels, unpredictability. Homework provides no such feedback. The ADHD brain genuinely cannot sustain attention the same way on low-stimulation tasks — it's chemistry, not choice.

Yes. Girls more often present with the inattentive subtype, mask symptoms socially, and are more likely to have their struggles mislabeled as mood or anxiety problems rather than ADHD. Diagnosis in community samples runs ~1.6:1 male-to-female versus ~2–3:1 in clinical samples — a real equity gap.

Not in the sense of the neurological differences resolving entirely. Overt hyperactivity often decreases, but executive function deficits typically persist without intervention — 60–80% still meet criteria in adolescence and 40–60% carry impairment into adulthood. Many teens do develop strong compensatory strategies with the right support, and the brain continues developing into the mid-20s.

commonlyAskedQuestions.q: Does my teen have something else going on too?
commonlyAskedQuestions.a: Very possibly — co-occurring conditions are the rule, not the exception (ODD, anxiety, learning disabilities, depression, autism, tics). A full psychoeducational evaluation, not just an ADHD screening, is the right next step if you suspect this.

That's a decision for you and your teen's doctor, not this dashboard — but the evidence is clear that combined treatment (medication + behavioral support) produces the broadest outcomes. Medication creates the neurochemical window for skills to be learned; it doesn't teach them on its own.

redFlags.title: Red Flags — When to Seek Additional Help
items: Significant withdrawal from activities they used to enjoy
Expressions of hopelessness, worthlessness, or not wanting to be here
Rapid or extreme mood changes beyond typical ADHD reactivity
Dropping grades combined with social withdrawal
Risky behavior that is escalating rather than stabilizing
Sleep significantly disrupted for more than two weeks
redFlags.clinicalNote: Adolescents with ADHD have approximately 3–7x the population rate of suicide attempts, largely mediated through co-occurring depression and substance use. Any report of self-harm ideation, hopelessness, or significant mood deterioration should trigger immediate referral.

openQuestionsForReview: Learning-disability co-occurrence rate differs between the Research Bible (20–30%, citing Mayes & Calhoun 2006) and the Parent Guide (~46%, uncited) — reconciled 2026-07-24 by keeping the citable 20–30% figure as primary; the Parent Guide's number is presented as an explicitly uncited softer claim, not a competing study.

jensen2001 citation for depression co-occurrence (15–20%) is referenced in the Research Bible's inline text but is missing from its AMA reference list. A likely candidate was found (Jensen, Hinshaw, Kraemer, et al., 2001, JAACAP 40(2):147-158) but the specific 15–20% figure could not be confirmed from the abstract alone — needs verification against the full text before citing as confirmed.
